items.summary: The existing theory of stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems focuses on open-loop and closed-loop solvability. For finite horizon problems, it is widely accepted that those two types of solvability are not equivalent in general, as demonstrated by explicit counterexamples. In contrast, they coincide in standard infinite-horizon formulations with constant coefficients under suitable stabilizability and integrability assumptions. This paper aims at challenging this well-established paradigm by developing a novel framework of closed-loop solvability, namely generalized closed-loop solvability, which removes the $L^2$-integrability constraint on the feedback strategies from the existing formulation. It will be proven that open-loop and generalized closed-loop solvability are equivalent and the classical closed-loop solvablity is a particular case only when the admissible feedback strategy is $L^2$-integrable over the time horizon. In other words, the previously established non-equivalence between open-loop and closed-loop solvability stems solely from the limitations of the classical formulation which requires the $L^2$-integrability of the admissible feedback strategies over the time-horizon. Therefore, this paper unifies the theory of the solvabilitiy for stochastic LQ control problems. Moreover, our results offer a novel insight to stochastic LQ control problems: open-loop/generalized closed-loop solvability is essentially equivalent to piecewisely local closed-loop solvability in the classical sense. The current paper is focused on homogeneous cases only and non-homogeneous cases will be studied in a subsequent paper.
items.title: A Unified Theory of Solvability for Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Control Problems I: The Homogeneous Case

items.summary: Active Microrobotic Sampling for Embodied Biological Digital Twins at the Limit STARLI Research Works  Institute XXVIII  Extension 06 English Description This high-density research monograph turns the biological digital twin from a passive recipient of measurements into an embodied experimental partner. Competing twins use uncertainty, expected information gain, physical reachability, safety, authorization, assay burden and traceability to propose the next microrobotic sampling location, time and analyte. The twin remains a versioned scientific belief rather than a replica of a patient, tissue or living system. Central Contribution The Active Sampling Evidence Charter binds twin ancestry, candidate and rejected actions, expected information gain, safety calculations, authorization state, robot trajectory, quantum and classical raw measurements, structured residuals, model forks, resets, abstentions and human overrides into one replayable evidence object. A quantum measurement qualifies only when it reduces biological sampling burden or improves mechanism discrimination against the best classical readout. items.summary: We consider the problem of Bayesian estimation associated to inverse problems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). In most cases of practical interest, one must use numerical solvers to implement computational methods based on Monte Carlo methods. This inevitably leads to an adaptation of multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods to reduce computational efforts to achieve a pre-specified mean square error (MSE). MLMC is based on sampling coupled versions of Bayesian posteriors associated to increasingly precise numerical solves of the PDE. In this article we present a novel method to implement MLMC based upon sequential entropic optimal transport couplings learned with light Schrödinger bridges, and correct the transport with Metropolis--Hastings steps that preserve the pairing. We bound the mean square error associated to a version of our new estimation method and show, for an elliptic inverse problem, that to achieve a MSE of $\mathcal{O}(δ^2)$ ($δ>0$) one can have an optimal cost of $\mathcal{O}(δ^{-2})$. The results feature explicit bounds on the effect of the fitted transport and of the Metropolis--Hastings correction. From a numerical perspective, on elliptic, Darcy-flow and Navier-Stokes problems, the method reduces the variance of the most precise solver by a factor of five to ten and is faster than multilevel sequential Monte Carlo [arXiv:1503.07259] at tight accuracies.
items.title: Sequential Entropic Optimal Transport for Bayesian Inverse Problems via Multilevel Monte Carlo

items.summary: Magneto-mechanical resonators (MMRs) are a recently introduced sensor technology for tracking and sensing applications that enables effective miniaturization down to the millimeter regime. However, estimating sensor parameters such as position from raw signals remains computationally challenging, because it requires solving a nonlinear inverse problem with computationally demanding objective function evaluations. In this work, we show how a deep learning method can accelerate this process by directly learning the inverse mapping from the measured signals. We consider the localization problem as an example and show that a convolutional-transformer regressor trained on simulated data with recorded noise can generalize to experimental data. The method achieves a median Euclidean distance error of 7 mm, which is comparable to the size of the sensor and corresponds to 6% of the size of a single coil. These results suggest that deep learning is a promising approach for rapid estimation of MMR parameters.
items.title: Data-Driven Localization of Magneto-Mechanical Resonators from Time Signals

items.summary: In this article, we propose ContactFlowFilter, a novel approach for contact estimation that determines the number of active contacts, their locations, and the associated force vectors. We consider a robot manipulator equipped with joint torque sensors and a base force/torque sensor; such a proprioceptive-only setup presents a challenging inverse problem characterized by (i) multi-modality from non-unique solutions, (ii) temporal dependencies in state evolution, and (iii) discrete contact events involving contact addition/removal. Existing approaches, such as particle filters (PFs) and learning-based methods, often struggle to address these challenges simultaneously. To overcome this, ContactFlowFilter integrates a generative model into the PF framework. The recursive structure of the PF captures temporal dependencies, while the flow matching model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events. Extensive validation in both simulation and real-world experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method. In real-world settings, ContactFlowFilter achieves the lowest dissimilarity from the target distribution, with errors of only 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm for single- and dual-contact scenarios, respectively, while operating at 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms.
items.title: Mixture of Flow Matching and Particle Filter for Proprioception-Based Online Contact Estimation

items.summary: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.
items.title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion

items.summary: We prove that the smooth affine hypersurfaces \[ X_{m,n}=\{ζ^mz_0^n+ (1+z_1ζ)z_2+ζz_3^2=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}^5,\;\; m,n\geq 2, \] have the density property. For every odd integer $d\geq 3$, we identify $X_{d-1,d}$ with a Kaliman modification along a Brieskorn variety of type $(d,2,2,2)$. We prove that the fourfolds $X_{d-1,d}$ are diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$ but not biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^4$. These, therefore, give counterexamples to the Tóth-Varolin conjecture.
items.title: A new class of smooth algebraic varieties with the density property and a counterexample to the Tóth-Varolin Conjecture

items.summary: The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™: Twenty-First Edition Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23547322 15 September 2026 | Revised 21 October 2026 Abstract Bias in artificial intelligence is not a technical accident. It emerges from choices about what knowledge is collected, whose language is centered, which categories are treated as universal, how populations are represented, what objectives models are trained to optimize, and who holds authority over the systems that result. The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™ is an operational decolonial architecture for identifying, interrupting, and replacing the epistemological and governance conditions through which Racial Empire Logic is reproduced in artificial intelligence. Rather than treating bias as a defect that can be corrected solely through post hoc fairness metrics, the Framework moves the site of intervention upstream into data formation, classification, model development, evaluation, deployment, and governance. Xam-Xam bu Gore: The Framework of Liberated Knowledge is the epistemological root of the DIA Framework. Authored by Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz and rooted in Wolof, Afro-Indigenous, and decolonial lineage, Xam-Xam bu Gore establishes that knowledge must exist in a state of liberation from colonial capture, epistemicide, institutional gatekeeping, extraction, and imposed hierarchies of intelligence. Its commitments to epistemological sovereignty, relational knowledge production, living knowledge, and liberation as the governing standard shape the Framework’s treatment of artificial intelligence as a knowledge system rather than a neutral technical instrument. The DIA Framework operationalizes these commitments through Four Pillars: Decolonizing Data Collection, Algorithmic Transparency and Accountability, Intersectional Impact Assessment, and Decolonial AI Governance and Accountability Mechanisms. Together, these pillars locate technical decisions inside their political, historical, cultural, and material conditions. The Framework requires attention to intersecting structures of race, gender, sexuality, disability, neurotype, class, caste, citizenship, language, migration, and colonial status, while rejecting the assumption that Western institutional categories constitute the universal baseline against which all other epistemologies must be measured. This Twenty-First Edition extends the Framework from governance-at-inference toward governance-at-formation through Decolonizing Large-Scale Self-Supervised Pretraining on Heterogeneous Corpora . The protocol identifies corpus construction, provenance, language representation, weighting, training objectives, and corpus revision as sites of epistemic governance. It advances accountable reclamation rather than archival purity, recognizing that knowledge survives through occupation, displacement, translation, institutional capture, resistance, and recovery. Its pluriversal approach seeks meaningful engagement across knowledge systems without requiring those systems to surrender their distinct epistemological structures to a dominant Western frame. Global participation is therefore positioned as decision-making authority over how knowledge enters, shapes, evaluates, and may be revised within an AI system. The edition also provides a corrected mathematical foundation for examining categorical incompleteness and intersectional disparity. Its formal results are deliberately bounded. They show, under stated assumptions, how aggregate parity across coarse categories can conceal disparities among finer community-defined groups and why any fixed category system may require continued refinement and governance. The mathematics does not establish universal elimination of bias, clinical validity, legal validity, ontological completeness, or the effectiveness of any specific deployment. items.summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
items.title: FHR File Converter

items.summary: Reliable evaluation of LLM-based alpha mining requires more than positive backtest summaries. We audit a preserved project at three levels: historical run counters, outcome retention, and a separately scoped public reanalysis. Three historical runs report 67, 20, and 11 keep decisions, but the comparison mixes metric populations: a mean over kept candidates is compared with a mean of per-round maxima, and successful evaluations with all returned outcomes. These artifacts cannot identify an architecture advantage. A released 1,837-expression catalog also excludes non-positive OOS outcomes, making its zero-reversal rate non-informative. We then account for all 1,047 unique expressions in a frozen, IS-screened preserved pool using forty A-shares and 2024-2025 rank associations. A versioned public-operator correction yields 923 scorable records, 99 with insufficient valid dates, and 25 unsupported, without modifying the other 990 prior diagnostics. Among scorable records, 671 have positive and 252 negative signed mean rank-IC. Simple untrained references also show positive associations, so this distribution does not establish incremental agent skill or profitability. The case study motivates explicit metric grains, immutable cohort accounting, and provenance-aware interpretation rather than architectural rankings from incomplete records.
items.title: Auditing LLM Alpha-Factor Mining: Metric Provenance and Full-Cohort Reanalysis

items.summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.
tags: backdoor triggers; poisoning rate; pretrained checkpoints; crop disease detection; before-after-cont
items.title: Backdoor-Trigger Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Disease-Detection Models Under Third-Party Pretrained Checkpoints: An Artificial Intelligence Poisoning-Rate Audit

items.summary: Nanoscale nonreciprocal elements are needed to control signal flow in scalable quantum technologies, but existing nonreciprocal components are often bulky. Here, we show that a strongly nonreciprocal current-voltage relation can arise entirely from coherent elastic scattering in a mesoscopic Rashba nanowire with gate-defined scatterers. We first identify the symmetry constraints that enforce reciprocal transmission in a phase coherent conductor even when inversion and time-reversal symmetry are broken. We then show how gates that are capacitively coupled to the leads, together with a magnetic scatterer or transverse subband mixing, can remove these constraints. In the weak-scattering regime, nonreciprocal conductance originates from interference between distinct backscattering paths. In the strong-scattering regime, nonreciprocity can be resonantly enhanced by the hybridization of the transmitting channel with bound states that arise from a higher transverse subband or spin-split band. In this regime, we find that a bias-induced change in the gate potentials of about one percent can produce an order-unity diode response, i.e., electrons are transmitted almost as in a clean wire for one bias polarity, whereas for the other polarity the current is strongly suppressed.
items.title: Quantum Interference Enhanced Rectification in Mesoscopic Nanowires

items.summary: Abstract (it)   Leonardo's Spatial Grammar è l’app che raccoglie le tre ricerche dedicate rispettivamente all’Annunciazione, all’Adorazione dei Magi e al Cenacolo: Leonardo's Rulers , Leonardo's CAD e Leonardo's Score . Non aggiunge una quarta indagine, ma riunisce i tre studi in una lettura unitaria, già depositata nel corpus accademico omonimo. Il corpus mette in discussione l’idea di un’applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana a base quadrata nell’opera di Leonardo da Vinci e propone, in alternativa, un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Dall’Annunciazione all’Adorazione dei Magi, fino al Cenacolo, emerge una grammatica spaziale in evoluzione: la rigida scacchiera lascia il posto a un sistema di righelli inseriti; la misura, inizialmente monodirezionale, diventa un’architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo è la retroingegneria CAD, applicata secondo il « banale aristotelico »: partire da ciò che l’opera mostra e che si può misurare. Bugne, mattonelle, arcate, arazzi e cassettoni non sono quinte, ma strumenti lasciati in vista, da cui le proporzioni — la progressione 1:2:3, il modulo 4:3 e i ritmi 1:4:1, 2:1:2 e 1:6:1 — si ricavano dalle stesse opere. Gli spazi restituiti sono misurabili, architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane. Le interpretazioni esoteriche e le simbologie non falsificabili restano fuori dal perimetro. L’app come strumento di lettura Leonardo’s Spatial Grammar riunisce le app dedicate alle singole ricerche e ne offre un accesso coordinato. Queste applicazioni sono strumenti di supporto alla lettura: facilitano l’esplorazione delle ricostruzioni, dei moduli e dei confronti geometrici, integrando la ricerca accademica senza sostituirla. App e studi costituiscono un sistema speculare in continuo aggiornamento: le revisioni della ricerca alimentano gli strumenti digitali e, reciprocamente, il loro impiego rende più immediata la verifica dei risultati. Spatial Grammar applica a Leonardo il principio che Leonardo stesso indica come fondamento del conoscere: prima l’esperienza, poi la ragione. La sequenza operativa è precisa: Pura Visibilità, esperienza, ragione, verifica. La Pura Visibilità consiste nel lasciare che l’opera si mostri prima di essere spiegata: nell’osservarne i segni sensibili senza imporre loro un significato. Segue l’esperienza, cioè la raccolta dei dati visibili — conci, cassettoni, gradini, allineamenti, proporzioni. Solo allora interviene la ragione, che riconosce moduli e ritmi; ma ogni ipotesi deve tornare all’immagine per essere verificata. Non si impone una griglia a Leonardo: si legge la griglia che l’opera stessa rende percepibile. Il Rasoio di Occam fa da cardine tra questa priorità del visibile e il metodo induttivo: non si porta la griglia all’opera, si ricava la regola da ciò che l’opera mostra. I segni sono visibili, i numeri e le proporzioni elementari. «Il Re è nudo!» diventa « Res patet ». Gli spazi sono ricostruibili, alla portata del CAD o di qualsiasi riga e squadra. Pura Visibilità: vedere prima di misurare, misurare prima di interpretare. items.summary: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation and Knowledge Transfer, represents the most significant recodification of the Czech RDI system in more than two decades. It replaces Act No. 130/2002 Coll., whose repeated amendments gradually reduced the clarity of the original framework and weakened its ability to respond to the changing needs of the research and innovation system. The Act constitutes a comprehensive reconstruction of the legal framework, complemented by Amending Act No. 329/2025 Coll. and implementing regulations. This article interprets the Act as a framework for a more investment-oriented governance of public support for RDI: in other words, as a basis for deciding how the state supports the creation, development and use of knowledge and innovation. Its key principle is the connection between excellence and impact. Excellent research is no longer treated as a value in itself, but as a precondition whose contribution must be demonstrable in terms of the country’s prosperity, security and international credibility. The Act therefore not only strengthens the capacity of research organisations to translate results into practice, but also opens space for instruments that may increase demand for knowledge, technologies and innovation. The text is not a legal commentary on the new legislation. Rather, it offers a sociological, historical and economic analysis that places the new legal framework within the broader context of the Czech RDI system. It is structured as a coherent arc: context – changes – implementation conditions – discussion – recommendations – conclusion.
items.title: Act No. 328/2025 Coll., on Research, Development, Innovation, and Knowledge Transfer: Recodification of the R&D&I legal framework in the Czech Republic

items.summary: This is a simulated photoacoustic data set based on the Monte Carlo Method using the simulation framework SIMPA. The simulations use a literature-based forearm model (see Appendix D of Schellenberg et al., Photoacoustics 28, 2022 ) and a digital twin of the MSOT Acuity Echo (iThera Medical). The generating script performs volume generation and optical forward simulation in 3D with MCX using 10⁸ photons and a spacing of 0.1 mm for 16 wavelengths (700 - 850nm in steps of 10nm). Acoustic simulations were performed on the central slice using k-Wave. Images were reconstructed with SIMPA’s delay-and-sum reconstruction algorithm (1540 m/s speed of sound, Tukey windowed bandpass filtering (0.1 - 8 MHz), and Hilbert transform envelope detection.  It comprises 1243 multispectral images in total, each of size 200 x 400 px containing these eight channels: oxygen saturation segmentation with classes: muscle, heavy water, blood vessel, epidermis, US gel, mediprene absorption coefficient scattering coefficient scattering anisotropy fluence initial pressure distribution delay-and-sum reconstruction
items.title: Simulated multispectral photoacoustic forearm dataset with reference initial pressure, segmentation, and vessel oxygenation maps

items.summary: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
items.title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories

items.summary: Thermal cameras enable robots to perceive human activities in darkness while revealing less personally identifiable appearance information and fewer details of the surrounding environment than RGB cameras. As vision-language models (VLMs), originally developed for RGB imagery, are increasingly integrated into embodied systems for scene understanding and high-level planning, thermal sensing offers a promising way to extend activity perception to low-light and privacy-sensitive settings. However, the failure modes of VLMs in thermal human activity understanding for human-robot interaction (HRI) remain underexplored. We fill this gap by evaluating seven locally deployable VLMs, including models developed for physical AI and robotics, on two person-centric thermal datasets. Our diagnostic tasks examine fine-grained action recognition, activity timeline reconstruction, and the ability to withhold unsupported answers. Paired RGB recordings serve as a performance reference, while controlled variations in frame sampling, thermal input presentation, and reasoning are used to assess whether the observed errors can be mitigated. Our results show that models can recognize broad activity categories but struggle with fine-grained actions such as coughing, sneezing, and yawning. They also produce inaccurate event timelines and hallucinate actions involving objects. Simple thermal input preprocessing and additional reasoning offer only limited, model-dependent gains. Abstention behavior also varies across models even under explicit instructions, limiting their reliability for practical robotic use.
items.title: Failure Modes of Vision-Language Models for Human Activity Understanding in Thermal HRI

items.summary: Anaxia, the BLLM engine, with the source, the Lean development and the checks of the paper BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI by D. Bhattacharjee and U. Bhattacharya. The engine is the Python package eBLLM (command anaxia ), a Lean 4 library and the container image ghcr.io/creelie/bllm-engine, which carries no model weights. The paper proves, in a model with independent runs, that certifying self-modifications costs an entropy (the entropy law), that a sound infinite self-improvement of finite cost exists exactly when one series converges, that a proposer needs a number of proposals set by a Rényi entropy of order one half, and that n verified layers sharing one budget cost at least n log(n/θ). Sixty-five of its theorems are proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib, each depending only on the three standard axioms. The engine combines known constructions in a typed crossing network with a program check and a refuter for every candidate, a shared memory and five target agents, and builds new objects in construction mode. Version 3.1.0 passes its mathematical-physics benchmark: every reflexive descent of each of the 473,800,776 reflexive 4-polytopes of the Kreuzer–Skarke list reaches a seed within 348 steps, so the Calabi–Yau seed conjecture holds; the sharp constants are 5 in dimension two and 11 in dimension three, and in dimension four the sharp constant lies between 22 and 348. The engine also learns from its failures: every failed attempt writes a record with its diagnosis and the one rule of the engine it changed, the loop is proved in Lean to stop, and a skill memory credits each change by the whole run it belonged to. The log holds 10 runs, 73 attempts and 57 rule changes, from the engine's own runs and from the attacks on simple zeros of the zeta function, the Erdős–Straus equation, union-closed families, lonely runners, the Dwork quintic, lattice Yang–Mills and points in convex position. On the Hodge conjecture, every convolution with at most seven line bundles on E 0 6 fails the polarised criterion at every discriminant, and so does every object supported on the 32 Weil threefolds. Version 3.2.0 adds the attack package for the four targets (barrier atlas, bypass search, superstring chain, the audit of a quantum-gravity manuscript, triage and the figure critic), the bridge index of 243 thirteen-crossing knots by transvection representations, and the constructions of the proof that gravity with the form factor of a scale-invariant brane gas has no ultraviolet divergence at any order of perturbation theory for n ≥ 4 (the brane response and its resonant refuter, the power counting, the one-loop tuning, the vacuum energy and the reflection-positivity refuter), each recorded as a CANDIDATE control until refereed. Version 3.3.0 adds the attempts of 21 October 2026 on the Hodge inputs (F2) and (F3') (three results and five construction rounds, all stopped on named walls), the proof that the mirror-fixed clause of the Geometric Selection Conjecture is empty, so that the conjecture is equivalent to a viable vacuum on a component carrying no standard embedding (control gsc-mirror-clause, CANDIDATE), two exact constructions from the TheoPhysEval benchmark, the final passes on Lehmer's totient problem and the brane gas, and a third pass on the knot tables that settles the nonorientable four-genus of 2,093 of the 3,525 open knots with 11 to 13 crossings (control crosscap4d-13, CANDIDATE). Of the six benchmarks only the seed conjecture is passed; the lattice Yang–Mills mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, the standard conjecture of Lefschetz type, Chowla's conjecture and Erdős problem 1183 stay open. The registry of the systems, methods and collections the engine draws on, with what it takes from each and what it leaves, is src/ebllm/bllm/data/sources.json and Appendix D of the paper.
items.title: BLLM: Beyond the LLM with Deep Human-Mind-AI

items.summary: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.
items.title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing

items.summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.
items.title: CloudIR-Bench: A Benchmark for Root Cause Analysis and Mitigation of Cloud Incidents

items.summary: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.
items.title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems

items.summary: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used as sources of knowledge for large language models (LLMs), hybrid AI systems, autonomous agents, and machine reasoning. However, conventional knowledge representation does not, by itself, establish whether a KG fact is ethically appropriate for a particular use, legitimately accessible to a particular agent, or endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. This paper proposes an EPB-passport framework that associates knowledge claims with explicit qualifications concerning Ethics, Privacy, and Bias (EPB). At the level of an RDF triple, the passport records whether a claim is appropriate for a specified agent or context, whether the agent is legitimately authorized to access or use it, and whether it is endorsed by a relevant epistemic constituency. These dimensions are distinguished from truth, provenance, and technical accessibility: endorsement does not establish truth, and technical retrievability does not establish legitimate access. The framework follows a conservative principle: a qualification must not be assumed merely because a claim exists or can be derived. Missing qualification information is treated as undetermined rather than as an implicit positive or negative judgment. The same principle applies to derived knowledge: an inferred claim cannot automatically inherit the EPB qualifications of its source facts but requires dimension-specific propagation and reassessment. The passport concept is also extended beyond RDF triples to semantic claims produced and manipulated by LLM-based systems, distinguishing computational units such as tokens and semantic spans from epistemic units such as claims and reasoning episodes. The paper develops and analyzes this conceptual and architectural framework, examining its implications for KGs, LLMs, LLM–KG hybrid architectures, and autonomous agents. Rather than reporting an implementation or empirical evaluation, it establishes a basis for explicit, context-sensitive governance of knowledge claims and identifies requirements for their formalization, propagation, and practical assessment.
items.title: Facts Need Passports: Governing Ethics, Privacy, and Bias in Knowledge Graphs

items.summary: The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™: Twenty-First Edition Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23547322 15 September 2026 | Revised 21 October 2026 Abstract Bias in artificial intelligence is not a technical accident. It emerges from choices about what knowledge is collected, whose language is centered, which categories are treated as universal, how populations are represented, what objectives models are trained to optimize, and who holds authority over the systems that result. The Decolonial Intelligence Algorithmic (DIA) Framework™ is an operational decolonial architecture for identifying, interrupting, and replacing the epistemological and governance conditions through which Racial Empire Logic is reproduced in artificial intelligence. Rather than treating bias as a defect that can be corrected solely through post hoc fairness metrics, the Framework moves the site of intervention upstream into data formation, classification, model development, evaluation, deployment, and governance. Xam-Xam bu Gore: The Framework of Liberated Knowledge is the epistemological root of the DIA Framework. Authored by Christian ZacaTechO Ortiz and rooted in Wolof, Afro-Indigenous, and decolonial lineage, Xam-Xam bu Gore establishes that knowledge must exist in a state of liberation from colonial capture, epistemicide, institutional gatekeeping, extraction, and imposed hierarchies of intelligence. Its commitments to epistemological sovereignty, relational knowledge production, living knowledge, and liberation as the governing standard shape the Framework’s treatment of artificial intelligence as a knowledge system rather than a neutral technical instrument. The DIA Framework operationalizes these commitments through Four Pillars: Decolonizing Data Collection, Algorithmic Transparency and Accountability, Intersectional Impact Assessment, and Decolonial AI Governance and Accountability Mechanisms. Together, these pillars locate technical decisions inside their political, historical, cultural, and material conditions. The Framework requires attention to intersecting structures of race, gender, sexuality, disability, neurotype, class, caste, citizenship, language, migration, and colonial status, while rejecting the assumption that Western institutional categories constitute the universal baseline against which all other epistemologies must be measured. This Twenty-First Edition extends the Framework from governance-at-inference toward governance-at-formation through Decolonizing Large-Scale Self-Supervised Pretraining on Heterogeneous Corpora . The protocol identifies corpus construction, provenance, language representation, weighting, training objectives, and corpus revision as sites of epistemic governance. It advances accountable reclamation rather than archival purity, recognizing that knowledge survives through occupation, displacement, translation, institutional capture, resistance, and recovery. Its pluriversal approach seeks meaningful engagement across knowledge systems without requiring those systems to surrender their distinct epistemological structures to a dominant Western frame. Global participation is therefore positioned as decision-making authority over how knowledge enters, shapes, evaluates, and may be revised within an AI system. The edition also provides a corrected mathematical foundation for examining categorical incompleteness and intersectional disparity. Its formal results are deliberately bounded. They show, under stated assumptions, how aggregate parity across coarse categories can conceal disparities among finer community-defined groups and why any fixed category system may require continued refinement and governance. The mathematics does not establish universal elimination of bias, clinical validity, legal validity, ontological completeness, or the effectiveness of any specific deployment. items.summary: Outcome-predictive signals are often treated as promising optimization targets in reinforcement learning, but predictive validity and optimization utility are different claims. We expose this distinction in GuanDan, a multi-round imperfect-information game in which the implication of a round outcome depends on the public match state. Held-out analysis shows that state--gain interactions provide incremental predictive value beyond a constant signed-gain effect, establishing that match progress is predictively meaningful. We then use changes in a frozen match-win predictor, $ΔΦ$, as a controlled round-level supervision intervention in a matched DanZero-style Monte Carlo self-play protocol. The intervention can succeed in an individual lineage: a selected progress-augmented checkpoint substantially outperforms its matched Baseline on a locked evaluation. Yet the method-level result reverses this impression: none of five preregistered replication seeds is positive, the pooled ten-seed interval includes zero, and across-iteration effects repeatedly change sign without a common late-stage advantage. These results identify a predictive--optimization gap: under the studied learner, a signal can describe outcome-relevant progress while failing to provide a reliably beneficial optimization direction.
items.title: The Predictive--Optimization Gap in GuanDan Self-Play

items.summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmar
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

items.summary: Third-party pretrained checkpoints are now the default starting point for computer-vision disease detectors in digital agriculture, yet the poisoning rate at which a backdoor trigger survives fine-tuning on clean crop imagery has not been characterised as a design quantity. the present analysis treats the backdoor trigger as a property of the checkpoint supply chain rather than of the attacker, and asks what poisoning rate a defender must assume when the provenance of the pretrained weights is unknown. A formal model of trigger persistence is developed in which the backdoor is represented as a parameter-space displacement whose survival under gradient fine-tuning depends on the ratio of trigger-aligned to task-aligned curvature. From this model a persistence bound is derived, and the bound is then embedded in a before-after-control-impact design that treats the poisoned checkpoint as the intervention and the clean checkpoint as the control. Operating characteristics were evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD of 6.0, residual SD of 4.5 and intraclass correlation of 0.64. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point difference at 80% power.
tags: backdoor triggers; poisoning rate; pretrained checkpoints; crop disease detection; before-after-cont
items.title: Backdoor-Trigger Evaluation for Computer Agriculture Disease-Detection Models Under Third-Party Pretrained Checkpoints: An Artificial Intelligence Poisoning-Rate Audit

items.summary: Differentiable logic-gate networks (DLGNs) are attractive for irrigation controllers because their learned Boolean structure can be verified exhaustively, yet the safety case for deploying them under actuator-failure cascades has not been formalised. The work is a design-and-power analysis of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation protocol, not an observational study: no field data are used or claimed. Operating characteristics were characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point compliance effect at 80% power under this variance structure, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the design's sensitivity. A formal-safety audit of DLGN controllers is then specified as a finite-state reachability problem over the actuator-failure cascade, with water-rights compliance encoded as an invariant. The contribution is a benchmark protocol that couples a verifiable controller class to a statistically defensible evaluation design, and a demonstration that the evaluation design, not the controller, is the binding constraint on regulatory acceptance.
tags: differentiable logic-gate networks; irrigation controllers; actuator-failure cascades; water-rights
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Differentiable Logic-Gate Networks for Computer Agriculture Irrigation Controllers Under Actuator-Failure Cascades: An Artificial Intelligence Formal-Safety Audit for Water-Rights Compliance

items.summary: Flood-risk mapping for agricultural insurance in vegetated terrain depends on computed-aperture radar interferometric coherence, yet canopy decoherence attenuates the signal that classifiers must detect. the present analysis formalises the detection problem as a before-after-control-impact design and derives the operating characteristics of a coherence-based flood detector under a declared variance structure with intraclass correlation 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation 6.0 and residual standard deviation 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 56 clusters to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The analysis characterises the detection-power bound that canopy decoherence imposes on payout-equity claims, showing that the cluster counts typical of agricultural insurance portfolios are insufficient to separate genuine flood signal from decoherence noise. The contribution is a benchmark-derived bound that links remote-sensing detection power to the actuarial fairness of index-based insurance payouts.
tags: SAR interferometry; coherence; flood-risk mapping; detection power; insurance equity; canopy decoher
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of computed-Aperture Radar Interferometric Coherence for Computer Agriculture Flood-Risk Mapping Under Vegetation Canopy Decoherence: An Artificial Intelligence Detection-Power Bound for Insurance Payout Equity

items.summary: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.
tags: federated learning; Byzantine robustness; crop disease classification; contamination bound; benchmar
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Byzantine-Robust Federated Aggregation for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under Adversarial Client Participation: An Artificial Intelligence Contamination Bound for Diagnostic Integrity

items.summary: Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.
tags: spiking neural networks; edge pest detection; thermal sensing; energy-accuracy trade-off; computer a
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Spiking Neural Networks for Computer Agriculture Edge Pest-Detection Under Thermal-Sensor Power Constraints: An Artificial Intelligence Energy-Accuracy Trade-off Audit for Field-Deployment Safety

items.summary: Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.
tags: tensor-train decomposition; model compression; plant disease classification; on-device inference; ac
items.title: Benchmarking Evaluation of Tensor-Network Compression for Computer Agriculture Disease Classifiers Under On-Device Memory Ceilings: An Artificial Intelligence Accuracy-Retention Audit for Field Diagnostic Safety
